HotLoop IoT first shipped in 4.18.10. The image is `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-iot:4.18.10`, built for amd64, arm64 and arm/v7, and the chart is `hotloop-iot` in the same Helm repository as the rest of the lineup. Both pull with no login. There is no Docker or Compose path, on purpose, and a bare `podman run` from a shell that dies with the session isn't an install.

Two ways in. A cluster gets Helm. A Pi, a NUC or a small industrial PC with no cluster gets Podman Quadlet. Either way the database is a choice you make once: PostgreSQL 16 (the default), or a SQLite file with no database container at all.

## Helm

```bash
helm repo add hotloop https://hotloop.io/hotloop
helm repo update
helm install hotloop hotloop/hotloop-iot --version 4.18.10 \
  --namespace hotloop --create-namespace
```

Call the release `hotloop` whichever product it is. The release name is what the database's volume, the Secrets and the Service are named after, and keeping it is what lets a site move up a product later.

That deploys IoT plus PostgreSQL 16.15 beside it on a 10 Gi volume, keeping 30 days of history. The chart generates the database password, the MCP token and an admin password into the release Secret, and reuses them on every upgrade, so a `helm upgrade` never rotates a password out from under you.

For a SQLite file and no database pod, ask for it when you install:

```bash
helm install hotloop hotloop/hotloop-iot --version 4.18.10 \
  --namespace hotloop --create-namespace \
  --set database.type=sqlite
```

SQLite is one writer on one local disk, so it is one replica, and the volume goes on local storage, never NFS. A site with years of history at one second wants PostgreSQL. The IoT chart takes `postgresql` or `sqlite` and nothing else: asking it for `timescaledb` fails the install. Moving between the two later is a backup and a restore, not a values change, because the new database starts empty. [Backups](/iot/backup/) has the restore.

### Back up the key

The chart also generates `<release>-secret-key` (`hotloop-secret-key` with the commands above). It holds the key that encrypts every password HotLoop keeps for a device. The key is never in the database and never in a backup, so it is part of your data: a backup restores credentials only where that key is mounted. The chart keeps the Secret through a `helm uninstall`. Back it up somewhere other than next to your backups, because a key sitting beside the backups it protects protects nothing. [Install the Gateway](/gateway/install/#back-up-the-key-before-you-need-it) has the whole story, and it is the same key.

### Sign in

The user is `admin`. The install notes print the command that reads the password back:

```bash
kubectl -n hotloop get secret hotloop \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.admin-password}' | base64 -d
kubectl -n hotloop port-forward svc/hotloop 8080:8080
```

Open `http://localhost:8080`. That admin account is a bootstrap, not a reset switch: once it exists, changing `auth.admin.password` and upgrading does nothing, so a password somebody set in the UI never gets clobbered by the next deploy.

Now add a device, discover its tags, and try to write to one. You can't. Writes ship off, every tag is read-only until somebody arms it, and `safety.allowWrites` stays `false` until you decide this deployment gets to move machinery. [The write gate](/gateway/write-gate/) has every check, in order.

### What to set before a real plant sees it

Put these in a values file and install with `-f`.

| Value | Default | Why you'd touch it |
|---|---|---|
| `plant.name`, `plant.siteId` | `HotLoop`, empty | What the plant is called on screens, in pages, and to other sites. |
| `plant.latitude`, `plant.longitude` | empty | Where the plant is, in decimal degrees. [The sun](/iot/sun/) is worked out from them on the box. Both or neither. |
| `global.timezone` | `America/New_York` | Schedules and shift changes run on it. It has to be a real zone name, because one that won't load stops startup. |
| `publicUrl` | empty | The address a phone on the plant Wi-Fi reaches HotLoop at. Without it, notifications have no link back and ntfy gets no Acknowledge button. |
| `safety.allowWrites` | `false` | The master switch. Off, nothing writes to a machine, from anywhere. |
| `safety.allowMcpWrites` | `false` | Lets agents write through the same gate. It narrows the master switch and never goes around it. |
| `historian.retentionDays` | `30` | Days of history kept. The Gateway and Edge keep 90, because a Pi's disk is small. |
| `logbook.retentionDays` | `90` | Days of entity state changes the [logbook](/iot/logbook/) keeps. |
| `database.postgresql.persistence.size` | `10Gi` | Your history lives here. Size it for your tag count and the retention above. |
| `secretKey.existingSecret` | empty | A Secret you manage holding the device password key. Set it if you render the chart with `helm template`, which can't generate a stable key. |
| `opcuaClient.persistence.enabled` | `false` | Turn it on before you add a secured OPC UA device, so the client's certificates survive a restart. |
| `ingress` | off | Only if you want it reachable from outside the cluster by a name. |

## Podman Quadlet

For a box that isn't in a cluster. Quadlet turns the containers into real systemd services: they start on boot with nobody logged in, restart when they die, and log to the journal. It needs **Podman 5.0 or newer**. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm ships 4.3, which has no Quadlet at all, so a Pi wants Trixie or newer. Put the database volume on a USB SSD and not the SD card, because history writes all day and SD cards die of exactly that.

The units are in the `iot/` directory of the HotLoop repository, under `deploy/quadlet/`. [Podman Quadlet](/install/quadlet/) explains what each file is. The short version for PostgreSQL:

```bash
sudo cp hotloop.network hotloop.container hotloop-db.container \
  hotloop-db.volume hotloop-data.volume /etc/containers/systemd/

openssl rand -hex 24 | sudo podman secret create hotloop-db-password -
sudo podman run --rm ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-iot:stable gen-secret-key \
  | sudo podman secret create hotloop-secret-key -
printf '%s' 'a long admin password' \
  | sudo podman run --rm -i ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-iot:stable hash-password \
  | sudo podman secret create hotloop-admin-password-hash -

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start hotloop.service
sudo systemctl status hotloop.service hotloop-db.service
curl -s localhost:8080/api/status
```

Then open `http://<this box>:8080` and log in as `admin`. The three secrets are the database password, the key that encrypts device passwords (lose it and every one has to be typed in again, so keep a copy somewhere that isn't this box), and the bcrypt hash of the admin's password, never the password itself.

For a SQLite file instead, use the files in `iot/sqlite/` and nothing from the directory above. They have the same unit names, so it is one set or the other, never both. It is two files, `hotloop.container` and `hotloop-data.volume`, and two secrets, `hotloop-secret-key` and `hotloop-admin-password-hash`. The database is `/data/hotloop.db` on the `hotloop-data` volume.

The unit follows `:stable`, and Podman moves it once the timer is on:

```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now podman-auto-update.timer
```

A new image migrates the database on its way up, and if it can't start, Podman puts the previous one back. The database container does not follow `:stable`, on purpose. [The :stable auto-update](/install/auto-update/) says what an update does, what a rollback cannot undo, and how to hold updates until you say. Take a backup before you turn updates on.

## Moving up a product

IoT to Edge to the Gateway keeps every device, tag, entity, automation, alarm, user and hour of history, and [the lineup](/products/) has the how. The Quadlet move has been run on one set of volumes. The same move as a `helm upgrade` on a real cluster, and going back down a product, have not been run, so don't take a box you care about down a product.

## What has and hasn't been run

IoT's SQLite Quadlet unit was run under systemd, rootless, from the committed files. The PostgreSQL unit, and the Edge and Gateway units, are generated from the Gateway's, which was run for real, and compared to it. A real Pi under systemd as root, and the 32-bit arm images on real hardware, haven't been done yet. This page will say so when they are.
